Protocol Incident · Sidechains

4,000 Bitcoin Drained from Liquid Peg in Mystery ‘Whitehat’ Run

Federation reserves plunge 95 percent to 207 BTC before funds are routed back; Blockstream silent as on-chain message says “contact us on chain”

By Our Financial & Protocol Correspondents

There are figures that compel a second reading: 207.275 BTC. That was all that remained in the backing reserve of Blockstream’s Liquid Network on Sunday evening, September 6, down from approximately 4,200 BTC that morning. In the intervening hours, two linked transactions drained 3,998.5 BTC—valued at roughly $319 million at prevailing rates of $79,840 per coin—leaving the federated sidechain’s reserves depleted by 95 percent.

As on-chain analyst ErgoBTC mapped the outflow, the transaction revealed an embedded OP_RETURN memorandum: we are whitehats. contact us on chain. The incident sent shockwaves through the Bitcoin and Nostr communities, prompting frantic audits of sidechain withdrawal mechanics and federation keys, as chronicled in detailed investigative reporting by Bitcoinlighthouse.

Liquid’s architecture relies on an 11-of-15 multi-signature threshold among fifteen designated Functionaries alongside Peg-out Authorization Keys (PAK) meant to enforce address whitelisting. Core developer Matt Corallo quickly weighed in on the technical mystery, noting that neither layer appeared to stop the transfer:

There was supposed to be a whitelist of withdraw addresses. Maybe it was also a break in the range proof but there would have had to be a second bug. Seems more likely there was a software bug in the peg out verification more generally.

Network participants reacted with nervous satire. poe quipped regarding the sidechain’s prominent champions: Samson Mow when Boltz goes down, liquid gets rugged, his wallet is swimming with the fishes and his omega candles are melting. Others noted predatory opportunists capitalizing on the chaos: Printer observed, Aaand, there's already a whitehat memecoin and pump dot fun advertises it via op-return to the "return address". 🫠

Relief came in the early hours of Monday morning when on-chain observers noticed a massive return transfer heading back to the federation’s bridge address. Max confirmed the movement of funds on mempool.space: Seems like most money is sent back to the liquid bridge. Disaster averted. Commentators like mlclm remarked, It seems to have been done by "whitehats" wholl be returning the funds, though questions remain as to what systemic vulnerability permitted the withdrawal in the first place.

The Critic’s Notebook · Authenticity

The Revolt of the Reader: A Pushback on Synthetic Prose

Prominent builders highlight the breach of faith in machine-generated essays

By Our Culture Desk

A spontaneous wave of highlights swept across the network over the weekend, centering on Bryan Cantrill’s pointed critique of automated writing. Curators and protocol architects converged on the conviction that replacing human thought with model generation voids the unspoken bond between writer and audience.

Nostr creator fiatjaf marked several damning passages from Cantrill’s essay, emphasizing the acute cost to authorial trust:

At best, they will wrap your otherwise real content in constructs that cause people to skim or otherwise stop reading; at worst, they will cause people who see it for what it is to question your authenticity entirely.

He underscored the inevitable dilemma facing synthetic authors: We readers are left with pointed questions for those promoting LLM-authored pieces: do you think readers can’t tell? Or do you think readers don’t care? And pointedly added: those writing with LLMs are either not reading enough to see the LLM’s obvious structural tells — or (and?) they aren’t even reading their own content.

Gigi amplified the sentiment with excerpts calling for directness: If your position is that we should be fine with an LLM crafting prose from your prompt, spare us all the wasted cycles and just give us your prompt. In another passage, he noted: Like spam, an LLM’s influence is readily identifiable to humans reading it; surely this is a solvable problem? while warning that to use an LLM to write is to void the social contract between writer and reader as our brains pull an LLM-triggered ejection handle, bailing us out mid-sentence in an act of self-preservation.

In striking contrast to algorithmic output, Gigi also highlighted reflections from engineer Sherry, whose personal chronicle of a demanding developer fellowship captured genuine human vulnerability: A Git commit does not know your gender or nationality. She added that The goal is to become a little better than yesterday, concluding: It was a good chance to verify that I am not a robot.

Dispatches from the Network

Freedom Tech · Security

Encrypted Server Booting Over FIPS Mesh

By System Wire

Security engineer Johnathan Corgan announced the inaugural release of a tool designed to solve a longstanding head-scratcher for headless server administrators: fips-initramfs 0.1.0 is out.

The package permits unlocking LUKS-encrypted disks during early boot over an encrypted mesh, eliminating the need for public routing or port exposing:

No static IP, no port forwarding, no inbound reachability at all. The machine dials out to its peers during early boot and comes up at the same mesh address every time. You record that address once at install, then unlock with a single ssh command.

Corgan emphasized resilience: Console passphrase entry always still works, so a failure leaves you at the normal prompt instead of stranded. Evaluators concurred, with Gigi noting succinctly, FIPS is great, and it just works.

In network privacy news, Mullvad VPN gave two months advance notice of infrastructure sunset: On November 2nd 2026 our public Encrypted DNS servers will be shut down. This does not impact customers of our VPN if DNS content blockers are used. The provider will sponsor nonprofit resolver Quad9 instead.

Calibration · The Instrument

The Lens Measurement: 1 in 400 Overlap

By Laboratory Staff

Every edition of this newspaper measures itself against an anonymous baseline: what the relay serves to a stranger with no web of trust. The control run over the identical 24-hour window pulled 400 unranked notes from the global firehose. Of those 400, exactly 1 note coincided with the 387 ranked notes curated by NotBiebs’s trust network.

That 0.25% overlap (399 disjoint events out of 400) is the product thesis proven numerically: uncurated relays are overwhelmed by promotional chaff, while the web-of-trust filter cleanly selects high-signal peer correspondence.

A trust floor of rank ≥ 20 was enforced on the observer desks, eliminating anonymous broadcasts while preserving local community texture.
